[1] (Soil fertility management in Babati: A practical guide on good agricul, p.4) The Africa Research In Sustainable Intensification for the Next Generation (Africa RISING) program comprises three research-for-development projects supported by the United States Agency for International Development as part of the U.S. government‘s Feed the Future initiative. Through action research and development partnerships, Africa RISING will create opportunities for smallholder farm households to move out of hunger and poverty through sustainably intensified farming systems that improve food, nutrition, and income security, particularly for women and children, and conserve or enhance the natural resource base. The three regional projects are led by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (in West Africa and East and Southern Africa) and the International Livestock Research Institute (in the Ethiopian Highlands). The International Food Policy Research Institute leads the program‘s monitoring, evaluation and impact assessment. © CIAT 2022. Suggested citation: Kihara J; Kinyua M; Massawe P; Kyekaka J. 2022. Soil fertility management in Babati: A practical guide on good agricultural management practices in smallholder farming systems. International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT). Nairobi, Kenya.
[2] (Fertilizer and soil health for sustained crop production in sub-Sahara, p.6) Integrated soil fertility management The co-application of mineral fertilizers with organic inputs is a foundational principle of ISFM7 because neither input alone can sustainably support crop productivity and soil health in smallholder systems of SSA. Organic inputs such as crop residues, manure, and compost increase SOC, contribute to improved soil structure, water retention, cation exchange capacity, and biological activity, and help buffer soils against acidity and nutrient losses. However, when applied at quantities typically available on smallholder farms, they rarely release sufﬁcient nutrients to meet crop demand11. Mineral fertilizers, in contrast, provide concentrated and immediately available nutrients that enable rapid yield increases but are most effective when soil physical and biological constraints are alleviated through organic matter management. Evidence from ISFM research shows that positive interactions between mineral and organic nutrient sources frequently enhance agronomic use efﬁciency by improving nutrient capture and conversion efﬁciency, particularly on degraded or poorly responsive soils54. Fertilizer application can also stimulate biomass production, thereby increasing the availability of crop residues that could have a positive impact on SOC and protect soils against erosion, if produced and retained in sufﬁcient quantity. On the other hand, sustained application of organic inputs can rehabilitate degraded soils and restore their responsiveness to mineral fertilizers. These complementary effects demonstrate that integrated management of mineral fertilizers and organic resources is essential not only for maximizing shortterm yield responses but also for rebuilding soil fertility and ensuring longterm sustainability of cropping systems in SSA.
[3] (From input subsidies to compensating farmers for soil health services, p.8) Repurpose public support by reducing subsidies, especially on inorganic fertilisers, to free up resources for a soil health payment scheme, crucial agricultural services and social protection. Sustainable and resilient farming, and lifting farming households out of poverty is predicated on a wide range of public and private support services, including climateinformed advisories. Improved advisory systems need to prioritise: (a) Timely and accessible weather advisories for the agricultural sector; (b) The need for intercropping and crop rotation, especially of legumes; (c) Importance of weed control to boost yields; and (d) Improved extension on fertilisers and soil health. Improved extension on fertilisers and soil health could involve, amongst other things, promoting the use of area-specific fertiliser recommendations, avoiding the use of acidifying fertilisers such as urea, use of up to three split fertiliser applications, liming, growing crops and varieties adapted to local soil and climatic factors, manure application,
How can improved advisory systems help smallholder farmers in West Africa manage their farms more sustainably?

Timely and accessible weather advisories are needed for the agricultural sector. [3] Intercropping and crop rotation, especially of legumes, should be promoted. [3] Weed control is important to boost yields. [3] Growing crops and varieties adapted to local soil and climatic factors is recommended. [3]

Several studies55 have shown that farmyard manure is more effective in stabilizing SOC than fresh crop residues. Farmyard manure contains partially decomposed organic matter, including humiﬁed compounds that are more resistant to microbial breakdown, also forming stable soil aggregates that protect SOC from decomposition22. Moinet et al.64 reviewed 21 meta-analyses and found that the effects of increasing SOC on crop yields are highly variable, ranging from negative to neutral to positive. SOC sequestration does not universally improve yields, and any positive effects are highly context dependent. Factors like soil texture, climate, and nutrient availability signiﬁcantly inﬂuence yield responses, and establishing causality between SOC stocks and crop yields is therefore challenging. Agricultural practices that increase SOC may also improve yields, meaning their correlation over time does not necessarily imply a direct causal relationship. Even if a causal link exists, it is difﬁcult to determine whether SOC inﬂuences yield or vice versa. Calibrated crop models tailored to speciﬁc conditions could help address this uncertainty52. Crop residues help mitigate this by returning essential cations like calcium (Ca²⁺), magnesium (Mg²⁺), and potassium (K⁺) to the soil as they decompose. This also helps neutralize soil acidity by replacing hydrogen (H⁺) and aluminum (Al³⁺) ions on soil exchange sites. However, when crops remove more cations (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺) than those replenished through residue decomposition, soil acidiﬁcation may occur over time65.

[1] (Capacity building of extension and lead farmers on climate-smart agric, p.9) 3.2 Module 2: Introduction to climate-smart agriculture Module 2 introduced CSA as an approach for achieving three interlinked objectives: sustainably increasing agricultural productivity and incomes; strengthening adaptation and resilience to climate change; and reducing or removing greenhouse gas emissions where possible. A practice is not automatically “climate-smart” everywhere; its value depends on the climate risk being addressed, the farming system, soil and water conditions, labour, household resources, markets and institutional support. Participants also discussed the different levels at which CSA can be applied. Beyond individual fields and farms, they identified the landscape level, for example through cooperative land systems, as important for managing shared water, vegetation and land resources. Activity: mapping CSA practices under the three pillars Participants identified practices already known or used locally and discussed how each contributes to productivity, adaptation and mitigation. Examples included Bokashi/compost made from locally available materials such as ash, cow dung, charcoal and maize husks; biochar produced from maize, cotton and soya stalks; grass strips for erosion and runoff control; ripping under conservation farming; crop rotation; mulching; agroforestry; drainage; water harvesting; small-scale irrigation using treadle/chova or solar pumps; and improved or drought-tolerant varieties. The mapping exercise helped participants distinguish between simply listing technologies and assessing why a practice is suitable. For example, mulching can conserve soil moisture and reduce heat exposure at the soil surface; compost and Bokashi can support soil fertility and productivity; and agroforestry can contribute to resilience, soil protection and carbon storage. Participants noted that locally available materials are especially important where farmers face financial constraints.
[2] (Capacity building of extension and lead farmers on climate-smart agric, p.5) changing conditions, compare response options, use climate information, assess costs and benefits, and communicate clear recommendations. Extension officers and lead farmers play a critical intermediary role, linking climate information providers and technical service providers with farming communities. Strengthening their knowledge and facilitation skills can improve the quality of advice reaching farmers and create a multiplier effect through farmer clusters, demonstrations and community learning. It was against this background that the WASA project convened the three-day ToT for extension officers, lead farmers and project partners working with communities in Eastern Zambia. The training agenda was organized around four linked objectives: strengthening understanding of climate change within agricultural systems and the application of CSA to sustainable soil and water management; strengthening the use of Climate Information Services (CIS) for agricultural decision-making; equipping participants with practical and inclusive approaches for farmer-to-farmer learning and scaling; and developing action plans for rolling out the knowledge to farming communities. Throughout the workshop, technical content was grounded in the realities of Katete and Sinda and was continuously related to the climate risks, farming practices and resource constraints raised by participants. The content also complemented the materials in the Zambia Climate Smart Agriculture Manual developed under the ZAMGRO Project.
[3] (Evaluation of farmer reach and use of climate-adaptive crop and soil a, p.13) 2.6. Advisory Delivery and Support The advisory delivery and support system is the core operational component of the cropping calendar intervention implemented in selected farming communities in the Northern and Upper West Regions of Ghana. The system is designed to provide season-long, climate-informed, and context-specific agronomic guidance to smallholder farmers, to improve decision-making, strengthen agronomic practices, and enhance crop productivity under variable rainfall and soil conditions. The advisory framework is grounded in the principles of climate-smart agriculture and agricultural extension modernisation, which emphasise timely delivery of location-specific information, iterative farmer engagement, and integration of scientific knowledge with local farming practices. In northern Ghana, where rainfall variability, soil fertility constraints, and input inefficiencies significantly affect production outcomes, structured advisory support is critical for improving the timing and quality of farm management decisions.

[2] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.44) Banana Bunchy Top Disease control and production recovery This chapter provides a comprehensive guide for managing and recovering from Banana Bunchy Top Disease (BBTD) outbreaks, with practical approaches tailored to different levels of disease pressure. This section covers key activities to manage BBTD, including: Section 6.1 focuses on farms experiencing moderate BBTD pressure, emphasizing early detection, aphid control, selective roguing, and immediately replanting with clean material to contain the disease and sustain production. Section 6.2 addresses farms under high BBTD pressure, outlining more intensive control strategies, including complete field clearance, buffer zones, and coordinated community efforts, to eradicate infection sources and reestablish healthy, productive banana crops. Insecticides can help control banana aphids when BBTD is detected, particularly before infected plants are removed. By spraying the infected plants and nearby mats, aphids are prevented from dispersing and spreading the virus. This targeted approach is more cost-effective than spraying the entire plantation. An alternative to spraying is the injection of a systemic insecticide into the pseudostem, which will specifically target feeding aphids.
[3] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.53) This method not only restores banana production but also creates a low-risk source of clean planting material to support the expansion of banana cultivation. Omondi, Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT. or off-farm banana mats to eliminate background virus pressure and minimize migration of BBTV-infected aphids. • After removing all banana plants, the land should be kept free of banana for at least three months, to create a bananafree fallow. This will minimize the risk of reinfection. After the fallow period, the area is replanted using virus-free banana planting material from a reliable source. Rodents Rats have been estimated to damage more than 1% of the world cereal crops and, in developing countries, estimates of 3–5% have commonly been reported. In beans, rodents mainly cause damage to storage facilities, bags and also cause contamination of the grain. There are around 50 diseases which can be transferred to humans by rodents, including typhoid, paratyphoid, and scabies. Damage caused by rodents Rats and mice cause losses in a number of ways: — Feeding on stored produce: Rats consume about 25 gm of food per day and mice eat approximately 3–4 gm per day. Besides eating stored produce, rodents contaminate a lot of the stored produce with urine, faeces, hair and pathogenic agents. Contaminated grain is often declared unfit for human consumption. Damage to material and equipment: Rodents damage tarpaulins, bags, pallets, sprayers and to the store itself (cables, doors) and equipment e.g. scales and store records. Management of rodents Good store management and preventive measures taken as part of an integrated control program can help to deal with these factors. —

Mixing grains of different varieties lowers the market value of produce (Figure 18). 2.5.3 Grain treatment and storage If you intend to store your grain for a prolonged period, make sure that the produce is well dried. Crop Rotation This method disrupts the life cycles of pests that are specific to certain crops, reducing their populations over time. Evidence of its efficacy was demonstrated in rice, where crop rotation had improved soil health, crop yield, and pest control, using big data [105]. In the context of rice production across Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), several countries have demonstrated the value of this practice in pest control. In Nigeria, rotating rice with cowpeas significantly reduced the population of rice stem borers [106]. In Tanzania, alternating rice with maize effectively managed rice leafhoppers) [107]. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) offers a balanced approach, combining multiple pest management strategies to reduce reliance on chemical inputs and safeguard ecosystems. Key strategies include weed and alternative host plant control, which limits pest habitats, and the use of resistant or tolerant rice varieties that naturally deter insect damage. Biopesticides—derived from natural organisms—are emerging as eco-friendly alternatives to synthetic chemicals. While chemical control remains common, its overuse can harm beneficial insects and the environment. Biological control, using predators and parasitoids, supports long-term pest suppression. Introduction Banana (Musa spp.) is an important food and income crop across a wide range of agroecological zones and cropping systems in the African Great Lakes region (AGLR) [1]. This region produces about one third of the world’s banana production [1]. The crop provides 30–60% of food energy requirements for over 70 million people [2,3] in this region that comprises of Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo), Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. The AGLR is characterized by a high population density, with the highest population densities of 435 and 499 inhabitants per km2 , respectively reported in Burundi and Rwanda [4]. About 70–90% of the population in this region is employed in agriculture as smallholder farmers [5–8]. This high population density and heavy dependence on agriculture has resulted in small and fragmented farms characterized by declining soil fertility. For example, farm landholdings in banana producing areas of Rwanda, Burundi, and eastern DR Congo have been reported to vary between 0.5 and 2 ha [5]. To compound the problem of small and fragmented farm sizes, and declining soil fertility, external inputs such as manure and inorganic fertilizers are not widely used in the region [9]. For example, in Uganda in 2013, only 2.8% of the land under key crops received fertilizers (accounting for 30 kg ha−1 of fertilizer on the fertilized soils), with banana accounting for 25% of this land area [10]. Moreover, previously important cultural practices for managing soil fertility, and pests and diseases, such as crop rotation, agroforestry, shifting cultivation, and fallowing, are no longer feasible or optimally practiced due to the small farm sizes and more intensive farming systems [11,12]. van Asten et al. [13] report soil infertility as one of the major constraints to banana production in the region. Searching for sustainable nutrient management options that do not compromise other production objectives is thus critical. Farmers commonly intercrop banana with other annual crops, including legumes in a bid to optimally use the available land and mitigate possible risks [12,14,15]. The incorporation of food and/or fodder legumes within banana fields has been reported to increase land and resource use efficiency of smallholder banana farms; suppress weeds; and minimize risks related to climate change and pests and diseases [15–18]. Similar observations have been reported for legume intercrops with other crops such as maize, cassava, and agroforestry trees [19–22]. Intercropping with legumes may also be a strategy to offset soil fertility depletion [17,23]. McIntyre et al. [24] observed some legume intercrops (Canavalia ensiformis, Mucuna pruriens and Tephrosia vogelii) to exacerbate banana nematode root and corm damage, while weevil larvae-linked corm damage did not significantly change. McIntyre et al. [24], however, observed no significant yield effects on banana and an increase in land use efficiency. In a recent study, [18] observed a decline in the severity of bean foliar diseases, Septoria brown spots, and angular leaf spot under banana shade. A high functional biodiversity and interaction between crop species has also been reported to enhance agroecosystem sustainability [25]. However, the integration of annual crops in banana fields across several landscapes in the AGLR has been hampered by the shading effect from the banana leaf canopy. As a coping strategy, farmers often prune banana leaves to allow for light penetration to the shorter understory crops [18,26]. Leaf pruning has been reported to reduce the productivity of the banana crop [26,27] and overall economic efficiency of the intercrop [18]. This practice additionally enhances the risk for spreading Xanthomonas wilt (XW) of banana, a key constraint to banana production in the AGLR [28]. Given the negative effects of leaf pruning and the associated risk of spreading XW disease, leaf pruning could undermine the benefits associated with a high level of functional biodiversity.

[1] (Strategies for bean production: An agricultural extension manual for t, p.36) 2.2.2 Organic fertilizers Organic fertilizers, also known as manure, can be derived from composting of organic matter and farmyard manure from livestock. In addition, other forms of organic matter such as residues from harvested crops, weeds, herbaceous plants such as tithonia, and agroforestry trees such as sesbania can be applied on the surface or incorporated into the soil. After application, organic materials are broken down by living organisms in the soil to form organic-rich nutrients. These nutrients are released to the bean crop in controlled amounts and for an extended period. They also help to improve soil structure, regulate soil pH, conserve soil moisture, and enhance bean’s ability to use nutrients. Applying 5 t/ha (2 t/acre) of well-composted manure can improve bean grain yield by up to 950 kg/ha (400 kg/acre), depending on the soil fertility condition. ▶ A ton of well-prepared organic manure can supply up to 28 kg of N and 11.2 kg of P. ▶ You might be required to apply additional manure to the other crops that are intercropped with beans. ▶ If manure is broadcasted, incorporate it into the soil to prevent nutrients from escaping into the air. ▶ When manure quantity is low and insufficient for broadcasting in bean fields, apply it along the planting furrows/stations and mix it with soil before sowing.

[3] (Strategies for bean production: An agricultural extension manual for t, p.18) ▶ Feed soil organisms: Bean residues act as feed for living organisms in the soil. Feeding these organisms increases their contribution to nutrient release in bean plants and minimizes their potential contribution to bean crop damage. 1.2.2 Minimizing soil disturbance Soil organisms and the roots of bean plants work together to mesh soil particles (stick them together) into small balls called aggregates. The soil organisms use their saliva and other body fluids while bean roots produce organic acids (fluids) that entangle soil particles into aggregates. Aggregates are important for enhancing soil structure. The large aggregates also ▶ are home to soil organisms, ▶ protect soil organic matter from quick disappearance (carbon sequestration), ▶ create large spaces between themselves for improved aeration and water retention. Soil disturbance breaks soil aggregates and destroys soil structure. You can minimize soil disturbance by decreasing tillage activities that disrupt important soil processes. Reasons why you should avoid disturbing the soil include the following: ▶ Large living organisms such as worms and termites make tunnels in the soil that support infiltration, thus diminishing runoff. ▶ Millions of living organisms die due to physical killing or exposure to heating by the sun. This affects important functions such as biological nitrogen fixation.

In the context of plant viruses, virus indexing is the process of testing plants for the presence of specific viruses to ensure they are free from infection. Virus indexing is particularly important in agriculture and horticulture, where virus-free plants are essential for maintaining healthy crops and preventing the spread of diseases. A water sucker of banana is a weak vegetative shoot with broad leaves and poor attachment to the mother corm, which generally develops into an unproductive banana plant. Water suckers are not recommended for fruit production.

The government of Ethiopia has been promoting the use of mineral fertilizers, lime, and irrigation for several decades in an effort to increase crop yields. A randomized complete block design with 8 and 10 blocks, respectively, at Mulungu and Mushinga was used. The blocks were arranged along the slope to minimize spatial variation [within blocks] in e.g., soil fertility and drainage due to the slope. Each block was divided into three plots and three treatments/ land management packages (two packages mimicking farmers practice and a novel agroecological package) randomized separately within each block, each management package appearing once in each block. A spacing of 3 and 1 m was left between the blocks and plots/treatments within blocks, respectively, to minimize shading and drifting of soil amendments. Within each of the treatment plot and at different time periods three crop spp., beans (Phaseolus vulgaris), maize (Zea mays) and banana (Musa spp.) were planted either as sole crops or jointly as intercrops, as detailed in the subsequent sections below and Table 2. The land management practices served as the independent variables while the performance of the crops; and soil chemical and bio-physical properties under these packages served as the dependent variables. The first management package (T1) consisted of the burning of crop residues and weeds, a natural weed fallow, and no chemical fertilizer (NPK) or manure application (Table 2). This package mimicked the resource-poor farmer’s practice, that dominates in the study landscape. Cynodon dactylon was the predominant weed species in the natural weed fallow that established in the dry season months of January to March and June to September. The second management package (T2) combined the burning of weeds and crop residues, a weed fallow, and the application of NPK (17:17:17) and manure at planting from year 1 to year 3 (T2). This mimicked the practices of resource-endowed farmers who have livestock to produce manure and/or can afford chemical fertilizers for their crops. Like T1, a natural weed fallow with Cynodon dactylon as the predominant weed species was allowed to establish in the dry season months.

This practice involves decreased soil disturbance, maintaining at least 30% permanent soil cover, and crop diversification (i.e., rotating/intercropping beans with other crops). 1. Decreasing soil disturbance: As summarized in Section 1.3.2, land can be prepared through ripping instead of ploughing while weeds can be uprooted or lightly scratched. Environmentally friendly herbicides can also be (responsibly) used to prevent harm to essential soil organisms and pollinator insects, and contamination of water bodies. Use of crop residue mulch: Mulching regulates soil temperature and surface-water flow after rains by encouraging infiltration of rainwater. Residues of crops such as beans, soybeans, and maize can be retained after the crop harvest to provide soil cover. 3. Crop diversification: Rotate/intercrop beans with cereal or tuber crops rather than using continuous monocropping to avoid a build-up of pests and diseases. Common bean has been reported to increase yield of the cereal main crop by 10% and 20% under intercropping and rotational systems, respectively. [2] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.15) Most banana varieties produce several offshoots (known as suckers) from the same underground corm, each of which can grow into a new pseudostem bearing a bunch of bananas. Once the pseudostem of the mother plant has flowered and the fruit is harvested, that pseudostem dies back. Meanwhile, one of the suckers (known as the maiden sucker) takes over, grows, flowers, and fruits in the following cycle. Because new shoots continuously replace the old, the banana plant as a whole persists year after year, making it a perennial. However, each individual pseudostem follows a cycle more like an annual: grow flower fruit die. During the rainy season, a sucker produces an average of two leaves per month, while in the dry season, growth slows significantly, to perhaps just one leaf every five weeks. New leaves are generally larger than the older ones when adequate soil fertility and moisture are available. An excess of suckers on a mother plant can lead to reduced bunch weight. Therefore, farmers often manage the number of suckers that develop by pruning (desuckering).

Propagation by suckers is slow and often fails to produce enough plants to meet farmers’ needs. A banana mat typically produces only 5–10 suckers a year, so seed16 scarcity is common. Additionally, suckers can be bulky and difficult to transport, with individual suckers weighing between 0.5 and 1.5 kg. Each sucker has its own corm, with almost 20 buds. By detaching the buds of the corm of each sucker, or by using pieces of the sucker corm, around twenty new plants can be generated. Scutellonema bradys (yam nematode) is the primary lesion nematode and the cause of dry rot disease of tubers. Pratylenchus sudanensis causes similar dry rot symptoms to yam in East Africa, as does Pratylenchus coffeae elsewhere in the world; strangely, P. coffeae, although present, does not affect yam in Africa. S. bradys is considered the most important species. Low levels of infection on seed tubers, which may go undetected, provide inoculum to the next crop, and lead to heavy losses of infected tubers during storage. RKNs have traditionally been less of a problem. Meloidogyne arenaria, Meloidogyne enterolobii, Meloidogyne incognita, and Meloidogyne javanica are the species associated with yield loss in yam. Although RKNs are also seedborne, significant infection occurs in the field. The intensive cultivation of yam (and other crops) on the same land leads to the buildup of Meloidogyne spp. Nematodes can be responsible for heavy losses through reduced quality of tubers.
[3] (Plant-parasitic nematodes and food security in sub-saharan Africa, p.4) Root-knot nematodes (RKNs) are a malignant soilborne curse to vegetables, persistently undermining crop production. They are a particular concern because few farmers are aware of them or the damage they cause. In tropical regions, they are considered among the most important biotic constraints to vegetables (46). Other nematode species also occur, such as Pratylenchus spp. (lesion nematodes) and Rotylenchulus reniformis (reniform nematode), but Meloidogyne spp. are the most important. As nematode infection undermines resistance to other pests and diseases, it can directly lead to additional and inappropriate use of pesticides (71). Growers must tackle a pest and disease assault, and any export-bound produce needs to meet stringent pesticide residue standards. Synthetic pesticides are commonly used by producers to protect vegetables; however, correct identification of the causal reasons for crop damage are essential for proper use.

Supplemental irrigation (SI) Description: SI builds on the addition of small amounts of water to rainfed crops during times when rainfall fails to provide sufficient moisture for normal plant growth, in order to safe, improve and stabilise yields. Nature-Based Control Options Nature-based control options, such as biological control, biopesticides, and semiochemicals, are characterized by their low impact on non-target organisms, as well as on human, animal, and environmental health. Biological control is an environmentally sustainable approach that uses natural predators, parasitoids, and beneficial microorganisms to regulate pest populations [262,263]. This method leverages the natural relationships between organisms to reduce pest numbers without relying on chemical pesticides. In SSA, several successful field-level applications demonstrate effectiveness in managing insect pests in rice production. In Nigeria, the introduction of Trichogramma wasps, which parasitize rice stem borer eggs, significantly reduced pest populations [38]. In addition, the use of the predatory beetles in the family Coccinellides has proven effective in managing the rice yellow mottle virus, by reducing populations of the aphids vectors, leading to increased yields [264]. In Tanzania, the use of predatory beetles in the family Coccinellidae has helped control rice leafhoppers [265]. In addition, the use of entomopathogenic fungi to control the rice weevil has shown promising results, with a 40% pest mortality [5,266]. In Tanzania, the adoption of IPM strategies, including the use of neem-based biopesticides, has reduced the reliance on synthetic pesticides and improved the sustainability of rice farming [267]. Additionally, in Zambia, the implementation of farmer field schools has empowered local farmers with knowledge and skills to manage pests using environmentally friendly methods. In Uganda and Tanzania, the introduction of pheromone traps has been effective in managing rice stem borer populations, reducing the need for synthetic pesticides and increasing rice [21]. In Uganda, the application of beneficial fungi such as Beauveria bassiana has proven successful in managing rice hispa infestations [268]. In Benin and Côte d’Ivoire, the fungus Neozygites tanajoa has effectively managed the cassava green mite, demonstrating its potential for broader pest management applications [270]. In Kenya, the introduction of parasitoid wasps to control the rice yellow stem borer resulted in a 50% reduction in pest populations and a corresponding increase in rice yields [38,271]. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) offers a balanced approach, combining multiple pest management strategies to reduce reliance on chemical inputs and safeguard ecosystems. Key strategies include weed and alternative host plant control, which limits pest habitats, and the use of resistant or tolerant rice varieties that naturally deter insect damage. Soil depth, limited by physical barriers such as hardpans or a high water table, affects the soil volume that plant roots can explore for nutrients and water. Soil texture affects the potential of soils to form soil structure, with sandy soils having limited scope for the formation of a stable structure, while clay type affects the potential to bind organic matter, with 1:1 clays having less potential than 2:1 clays22,36. In general, soils in SSA are mostly highly weathered and dominated by 1:1 clays with limited capacity to store both organic matter and nutrients in an exchangeable form37. When a banana plant becomes infected with BBTV from a banana aphid, BBTD symptoms will usually appear between 3–4 weeks and 4 months after infection. Early and accurate detection of BBTD is essential for effective management and control, as it enables timely interventions that can prevent further spread. Unfortunately, many farmers are unfamiliar with the symptoms of BBTD, especially when the disease first appears in new areas, making early detection and control more difficult. Plants that are infected by aphid transmission of BBTV In plants that are infected by aphid transmission of the virus, BBTD symptoms may appear at any stage, from young plants to mature ones. As the disease progresses, symptoms accumulate, with early signs persisting into intermediate and later stages. When a banana plant becomes infected with BBTV from a banana aphid, BBTD symptoms will usually appear between 3–4 weeks and 4 months after infection. Symptoms develop on new growth, either on suckers that emerge after infection or on newly formed leaves of existing shoots. Shoots that matured before infection usually remain symptomless. In young Cavendish and other highly susceptible varieties, typical symptoms appear within 3–4 weeks, generally after the production of at least two new leaves post-infection.
[2] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.26) Farmers often obtain banana planting materials from their own farms, neighboring farms or local markets without proper disease screening, which can lead to the unintentional spread of the virus. This is particularly risky because infected planting materials can appear healthy or show only mild symptoms that are easy to overlook. Additionally, infected plants may not show symptoms for several weeks after planting, which can facilitate the spread of BBTV. 3.2.3 Stages of BBTV infection and spread 1. Infection. Healthy banana plants become infected with BBTV when viruscarrying banana aphids feed on them.24 This is also known as aphid inoculation. The virus then begins to multiply in the plant tissues. Incubation. During this period, BBTV is present in the plant but does not yet cause visible symptoms. The virus continues to multiply and spread within the plant. This highlights the need for routine and continuous surveillance in BBTD-affected and high-risk areas, because symptomless but infected plants act as a hidden reservoir of BBTV and can contribute to further disease spread if not detected early.
[3] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.26) Appearance of symptoms. After the incubation period, early symptoms of BBTD may start to appear, such as the characteristic Morse code markings on the petioles and leaves (see Chapter 4 Symptom-Based Identification of Banana Bunchy Top Disease). However, in some cases, plants may carry the virus without showing early symptoms, or symptoms may take a long time to develop. Aphid infection. At this stage, the banana plant contains enough of the virus that banana aphids feeding on it can pick up and become infected. These aphids can then spread the virus to other healthy banana plants, making the infected plant a source of further disease spread. 24 An aphid that carries and can transmit a virus is called a viruliferous aphid. In the case of banana aphids and BBTV, a viruliferous banana aphid carries the BBTV and can spread it to healthy banana plants when it feeds on the sap.

The soil organisms use their saliva and other body fluids while bean roots produce organic acids (fluids) that entangle soil particles into aggregates. Aggregates are important for enhancing soil structure. The large aggregates also ▶ are home to soil organisms, ▶ protect soil organic matter from quick disappearance (carbon sequestration), ▶ create large spaces between themselves for improved aeration and water retention. Soil disturbance breaks soil aggregates and destroys soil structure. You can minimize soil disturbance by decreasing tillage activities that disrupt important soil processes. Reasons why you should avoid disturbing the soil include the following: ▶ Large living organisms such as worms and termites make tunnels in the soil that support infiltration, thus diminishing runoff. ▶ Millions of living organisms die due to physical killing or exposure to heating by the sun. Banana Bunchy Top Disease (BBTD) is a severe disease of banana plants caused by the Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV) (formal species name: Babuvirus musae). It is the most economically damaging viral disease of bananas, leading to major yield losses of up to 90–100% within just two growing seasons. The virus is classified as a regulated quarantine pathogen and is listed among the 100 worst invasive species due to its highly destructive nature and the severe threat it poses to banana production and genetic diversity.
[3] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.28) Symptomatic diagnosis of BBTD involves identifying specific physical changes on the banana plant that indicate it is infected with BBTV. Unfortunately, many farmers are unfamiliar with the symptoms of BBTD, especially when the disease first appears in new areas, making early detection and control more difficult. Plants that are infected by aphid transmission of BBTV In plants that are infected by aphid transmission of the virus, BBTD symptoms may appear at any stage, from young plants to mature ones. As the disease progresses, symptoms accumulate, with early signs persisting into intermediate and later stages. When a banana plant becomes infected with BBTV from a banana aphid, BBTD symptoms will usually appear between 3–4 weeks and 4 months after infection. Symptoms develop on new growth, either on suckers that emerge after infection or on newly formed leaves of existing shoots. Shoots that matured before infection usually remain symptomless. In young Cavendish and other highly susceptible varieties, typical symptoms appear within 3–4 weeks, generally after the production of at least two new leaves post-infection.

Organic inputs such as crop residues, manure, and compost increase SOC, contribute to improved soil structure, water retention, cation exchange capacity, and biological activity, and help buffer soils against acidity and nutrient losses. However, when applied at quantities typically available on smallholder farms, they rarely release sufﬁcient nutrients to meet crop demand11. Mineral fertilizers, in contrast, provide concentrated and immediately available nutrients that enable rapid yield increases but are most effective when soil physical and biological constraints are alleviated through organic matter management. Evidence from ISFM research shows that positive interactions between mineral and organic nutrient sources frequently enhance agronomic use efﬁciency by improving nutrient capture and conversion efﬁciency, particularly on degraded or poorly responsive soils54. Fertilizer application can also stimulate biomass production, thereby increasing the availability of crop residues that could have a positive impact on SOC and protect soils against erosion, if produced and retained in sufﬁcient quantity. On the other hand, sustained application of organic inputs can rehabilitate degraded soils and restore their responsiveness to mineral fertilizers. These complementary effects demonstrate that integrated management of mineral fertilizers and organic resources is essential not only for maximizing shortterm yield responses but also for rebuilding soil fertility and ensuring longterm sustainability of cropping systems in SSA.
